prompt: ELINT is a SIGINT sub-discipline dedicated to collecting and analysing which kind of signals?
explanation: Slide 5 quotes PAM 3-0702-01: ELINT is a specialized SIGINT sub-discipline for non-communication electromagnetic signals. Slide 7 gives voice, text and data messages to COMINT.

prompt: The two sub-disciplines of SIGINT are
explanation: Slide 6 divides SIGINT, the intelligence arm, into COMINT and ELINT, and Slide 24 asks for exactly this pair. ES, EA and EP belong to EW, the action arm.

prompt: Why can an enemy receiver find a radar?
options: It must transmit to work, and every transmission can be found
Its weak echo is intercepted at the enemy receiver
It is switched to track, which exposes it
Counter-battery radars are the only emitters that can be found
explanation: Slide 5 states that a radar has to transmit to work and every transmission can be found. Slide 10 shows ELINT intercepts the loud outgoing pulse, not the weak echo.

prompt: Which of the following correctly pairs a discipline with the signals it covers?
options: ELINT - voice, text and data messages
COMINT - signals that carry no messages
explanation: Slide 7 pairs COMINT with voice, text and data messages and ELINT with radars, beacons and sensors.

prompt: ELINT mainly answers which question?
options: What does the enemy intend by this message?
Which friendly net is suffering interference?
What equipment is it, where is it, and what is it doing?
How quickly must the commander act on this warning?
explanation: Slide 7 gives ELINT the question "What equipment, where, doing what?", while COMINT asks what the enemy intends.

prompt: ES and ELINT teams may use the same receiver. According to the lesson, what separates their work?
options: Which frequency band each team may search
Whether the emitter is friendly or adversary
Whether the signal is a radar or a radio
Who tasked the collection and what the product is for
explanation: Slide 8 describes the same receiver with a different "why": who tasked it and what the product is for. Radar versus radio separates ELINT from COMINT on Slide 7.

prompt: A catalogue of the unit's own radios, radars, data links and navigation aids belongs to which Electronic Order of Battle?
explanation: Slide 9 names three EOBs; the Friendly EOB lists our own emitters. The Adversary EOB holds hostile emitters and the Neutral EOB holds civilian and commercial ones.

prompt: A maritime-distress radio and an air traffic control radar are logged near the coast. Which EOB holds them?
explanation: Slide 9 places civilian and commercial emitters such as air traffic control and maritime distress in the Neutral EOB.

category: Radar Principles and the One-Way Advantage
prompt: On a waterfall trace, short hits spaced at exact, even intervals most likely come from
explanation: Slide 4 reads evenly spaced short hits as a beam sweeping past once per rotation: people talk irregularly, machines repeat.

category: Radar Principles and the One-Way Advantage
prompt: In the lesson's radar sequence of pulse out and echo back, time equals
explanation: Slide 10 summarises the sequence as pulse out, echo back, time equals range.

category: Radar Principles and the One-Way Advantage
prompt: A receiver can usually detect a radar from beyond the radar's own detection range because the receiver
options: Needs the echo as well as the pulse
Is invisible to every other receiver
Hears a stronger pulse than the radar does
Needs only the outbound trip of the pulse
explanation: Slide 11 explains the one-way advantage: the radar needs its weak echo back over a two-way trip, while a receiver needs only the outbound trip.

prompt: Which radar fingerprint parameter gives the orientation of the wave?
explanation: Slide 12 lists polarization as the orientation of the wave. Modulation and bandwidth is the shape of the signal inside the pulse.

prompt: A radar with a PRI of 1 ms has a PRF of
explanation: Slide 13 gives PRF = 1 divided by PRI, and Slide 24 answers this case: a PRI of 1 ms is a PRF of 1 kHz.

prompt: A new emitter has a carrier frequency of 5 GHz. In which NATO radar band does it fall?
explanation: Slide 13 notes that the carrier frequency tells you the band, and Slide 17 lists G-band as 4-6 GHz.

prompt: Which parameter of a radar fingerprint tells how long each single pulse lasts?
explanation: Slide 13 defines PW as how long each pulse lasts. PRI is the time between pulses.

prompt: A circular scan is
options: A back-and-forth search over one area of interest
A beam held steadily on one target
A wide beam that covers more area faster
A 360-degree search that sweeps the whole area like a lighthouse
explanation: Slide 15 describes a circular scan as a 360-degree search like a lighthouse. A sector scan goes back and forth over an area of interest.

prompt: A beam that sweeps past once per rotation, with a lower PRF and a longer PW, is read by the lesson as
options: Track: the radar is aiming at someone
Search: the radar is looking around the area
Beacon: a transmitter is being left on
Data link: short wideband bursts are being sent
explanation: Slide 16 reads a rotating or sector scan with a lower PRF and a longer PW as search. Track is a steady beam with a higher PRF and shorter PW.

prompt: Which ground emitter detects people and vehicles moving at range?
explanation: Slide 18 lists the ground-surveillance radar as detecting people and vehicles moving at range. The weapon-locating radar detects incoming shells.

prompt: The third step of the ES and ELINT process, where the fingerprint of Ft, PW, PRI and scan is measured, is
explanation: Slide 19 makes Analyse the third step. Evaluate follows and matches the measurements against the signature library.

prompt: Into what does ES data feed so that emitters can be matched with EA, cyber or kinetic responses?
explanation: Slide 22 says ES data feeds the targeting board to match emitters with responses. The signature library on Slide 20 is the record set of intercepts.
